lessons.title: Percentages
lessons.subject: Math
learning_objectives: Understand percentage as parts per hundred
lessons.reading_material: Percent means 'per hundred'. 50% means 50 out of 100, or 1/2. 25% = 25/100 = 1/4. To find 30% of 80: 80 × 30 ÷ 100 = 24. Percentages are everywhere: discounts in shops, test scores, statistics. Key conversions: 1/2=50%, 1/4=25%, 3/4=75%, 1/5=20%, 1/10=10%.
practical_activities: VAT calculation role play
Sale discount problems
Statistics and percentages from data

revision.notes: Percentage: n% of x = (n/100) × x. Convert: fraction → decimal → percentage (×100).
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Ratio and Proportion
lessons.subject: Math
lessons.reading_material: A RATIO compares two quantities. If there are 3 boys and 5 girls, the ratio of boys to girls is 3:5. We can also write 3/5 or 'three to five'. Ratios can be simplified like fractions: 6:10 = 3:5. PROPORTION means two ratios are equal. If 2 books cost £6, then 5 books cost £15 (same ratio: £3 per book).
practical_activities: Mix paint colours using ratios
Map scale reading
Recipe scaling (double/halve quantities)

exercises.q: If 3 apples cost 90p, how much do 7 cost?

homework.task: Find the ratio of vowels to consonants in your full name. Simplify it.

revision.notes: Ratio a:b means a for every b. Simplify by dividing both by HCF. Proportion: unit rate method.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Statistics: Mean, Median, Mode
lessons.subject: Math
lessons.reading_material: MEAN = sum ÷ count (the balance point). MEDIAN = middle value when ordered (not affected by extremes). MODE = most common value. Example data: 4, 7, 3, 7, 9. Ordered: 3,4,7,7,9. Mean=(4+7+3+7+9)÷5=30÷5=6. Median=7 (middle). Mode=7 (appears twice). Choose based on purpose!
practical_activities: Calculate class average heights
Find median shoe size
Mode in favourite colour survey

homework.task: Record 7 temperatures this week. Calculate mean, find median and mode.

revision.notes: Mean: sum÷count. Median: middle (or avg of 2 middle). Mode: most frequent. Use median for skewed data.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.subject: English
learning_objectives: Identify narrative techniques (show don't tell, dialogue, flashback)
lessons.reading_material: 'SHOW, DON'T TELL' means using details rather than stating emotions: instead of 'She was scared', write 'Her hands trembled and her heart hammered'. Authors use these techniques deliberately to create effects.

lessons.title: Cells: The Building Blocks of Life
lessons.subject: Science
learning_objectives: Describe the structure of animal and plant cells
lessons.reading_material: All living things are made of cells. Animal cells have a nucleus (control centre), cell membrane (boundary), and cytoplasm (jelly-like fluid). Plant cells also have a cell wall (rigid outer layer) and chloroplasts (for photosynthesis).
practical_activities: Draw and label animal and plant cells

revision.notes: Plant cells have cell wall + chloroplasts; animal cells do not.

lessons.title: Climate Change
lessons.subject: Geography
learning_objectives: Describe the causes and effects of climate change
lessons.reading_material: The greenhouse effect keeps Earth warm naturally. But burning fossil fuels releases excess CO₂, trapping more heat. This causes global warming: rising temperatures, melting ice caps, sea level rise, more extreme weather. Solutions: reduce emissions, renewable energy, reforestation.
practical_activities: Graph temperature data over 100 years
Debate: what can students do about climate change?

exercises.q: What gas is mainly responsible for enhanced greenhouse effect?

homework.task: Calculate your family's approximate carbon footprint for one week

revision.notes: More CO₂ = more heat trapped = global warming = climate change.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

questions.q: What is one effect of global warming?

lessons.title: Trade and Globalisation
lessons.subject: Geography
learning_objectives: Describe how globalisation connects the world
lessons.reading_material: Countries trade goods and services because no country has everything it needs. Exports = goods sold to other countries. Imports = goods bought from other countries. Globalisation = increasing connection between countries through trade, technology, and culture. Multinational companies operate in many countries.
practical_activities: Trace where your phone/shoes were made
Research a supply chain for a common product

homework.task: List 10 products in your home and find where each was made

revision.notes: Export = sell abroad. Import = buy from abroad. Globalisation connects economies.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: The Renaissance
lessons.subject: World History
learning_objectives: Identify key Renaissance figures and their contributions
lessons.reading_material: The Renaissance (14th–17th century) was a cultural rebirth in Europe beginning in Italy. Artists rediscovered classical Greek and Roman ideas. Leonardo da Vinci: art and science. Michelangelo: sculpture and painting (Sistine Chapel). Gutenberg's printing press (1440) spread ideas rapidly. Humanism: focus on human reason and potential.
practical_activities: Analyse Renaissance vs medieval art
Re-create a Leonardo sketch

homework.task: Research one Renaissance invention and explain how it changed society

revision.notes: Renaissance = rebirth of classical ideas. Italy first. Key: humanism, art, science, printing press.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Age of Exploration
lessons.subject: World History
learning_objectives: Describe the motivations for European exploration
Evaluate the impact of colonisation on indigenous peoples
lessons.reading_material: From the 15th century, European nations explored the world seeking trade routes, gold, and glory. Columbus reached the Americas in 1492. Vasco da Gama sailed to India. Magellan's crew first circumnavigated the globe. European colonisation brought diseases that devastated indigenous populations, forced labour, and cultural destruction — alongside trade and exchange.
practical_activities: Map key exploration voyages
Debate: was European exploration a good or bad thing?

exercises.q: Who first reached the Americas in 1492?

homework.task: Research how colonisation affected one indigenous culture

revision.notes: Exploration: glory, god, gold. Columbus 1492. Colonisation = exploitation and cultural destruction.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

options: Many died from disease and exploitation
questions.answer: Many died from disease and exploitation

lessons.title: Akhlaq — Islamic Character
lessons.subject: Islamic Studies
learning_objectives: Apply Islamic values to everyday situations
lessons.reading_material: Akhlaq means moral character and ethical behaviour in Islam. Key virtues: honesty (sidq), generosity (karam), patience (sabr), justice (adl), and mercy (rahma). The Quran and Sunnah provide guidance on how to treat others with excellence (Ihsan).
practical_activities: Case studies: how would a Muslim with good akhlaq respond to each situation?
Design an 'Islamic values' classroom poster
exercises: Define 3 Islamic virtues in your own words
Give one example of how to show patience in daily life
lessons.homework: Write a reflection on one Islamic virtue you want to develop and your plan to practise it.

revision.notes: Ihsan means doing everything with excellence and awareness that Allah sees all actions.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.reading_material: Poetry exists in every culture and language. Pablo Neruda (Chile) wrote passionate love poems and political verse. Rabindranath Tagore (India) won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913 for 'Gitanjali'. Mahmoud Darwish (Palestine) expressed longing for homeland. Matsuo Bashō (Japan) perfected the haiku form (5-7-5 syllables). Emily Dickinson (USA) wrote quiet, powerful poems about death and nature. Poetic devices: simile (like/as), metaphor (direct comparison), imagery (sensory language), personification (giving human traits to objects).
practical_activities: Write a haiku inspired by nature; read aloud a poem from a culture different from your own
exercises: Name 3 poetic devices and give an example of each
Write a haiku on the topic of rain
Who was Rabindranath Tagore?
lessons.homework: Read one poem by Neruda or Darwish — write a 3-sentence response explaining its emotion.

revision.notes: Simile = like/as. Metaphor = direct comparison. Haiku = 5-7-5 syllables. Tagore = Nobel laureate.
revision.tip: Read poetry aloud — the sound reveals meaning.

lessons.title: Perspective and Composition
lessons.subject: Art
learning_objectives: Use the rule of thirds in composition
lessons.reading_material: Perspective creates the illusion of depth. One-point perspective: parallel lines converge at a vanishing point. Renaissance artists like Leonardo mastered perspective.

learning_objectives: Play or sing a simple chord progression
lessons.reading_material: HARMONY is when two or more notes sound together. A CHORD is three or more notes played at the same time. Major chords sound happy and bright; minor chords sound sad or serious. The I-IV-V-I progression is used in hundreds of songs.

lessons.title: Water Safety and Drowning Prevention
lessons.subject: Survival Skills
learning_objectives: Know how to call for help near water
lessons.reading_material: Drowning is one of the leading causes of accidental death in children. Never swim alone — always have a buddy. Rip currents: if caught, swim parallel to the shore, not against the current. H.E.L.P. position (Heat Escape Lessening Posture): pull knees to chest to conserve body heat in cold water. If someone is in trouble: do not enter the water — throw a rope, life ring, or floating object. Call for help immediately.
practical_activities: Demonstrate HELP position in a swimming pool or practice on land with diagrams
exercises: What is a rip current and how should you escape it?
Explain the HELP position and when to use it
Why should you never swim alone?
lessons.homework: Research water safety rules at your nearest beach or swimming pool and present them to the class.

revision.notes: Never swim alone. Rip current: swim parallel to shore. HELP position conserves heat. Throw, don't go.
revision.tip: 'Throw, Don't Go' — throwing a flotation aid is safer than jumping in to rescue someone.

options: Swim parallel to the shore then back in
quiz.correct: Swim parallel to the shore then back in

quiz.question: The HELP position is used to
options: Conserve body heat in cold water
quiz.correct: Conserve body heat in cold water

lessons.assessment: Write a water safety leaflet with 5 rules and an explanation of the HELP position.

info_cards.fact: "He who has a why to live can bear almost any how." — Friedrich Nietzsche, German philosopher.

info_cards.title: Famous Quote
info_cards.fact: "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind." — Neil Armstrong, astronaut.

info_cards.title: Famous Person: Nelson Mandela
info_cards.fact: Nelson Mandela spent 27 years in prison for opposing apartheid in South Africa and later became the country's first democratically elected president.

info_cards.title: Book Summary: Sapiens
info_cards.fact: "Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind" by Yuval Noah Harari (2011) traces the history of the human species from prehistoric foragers to the modern world.

info_cards.title: Book Summary: The Wright Brothers
info_cards.fact: "The Wright Brothers" by David McCullough tells the true story of how Orville and Wilbur Wright invented and flew the first successful airplane.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Stephen Hawking
info_cards.fact: "However difficult life may seem, there is always something you can do and succeed at." — British theoretical physicist known for his work on black holes and his book A Brief History of Time.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Carl Sagan
info_cards.fact: "Somewhere, something incredible is waiting to be known." — American astronomer and science communicator who hosted the television series Cosmos.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Richard Feynman
info_cards.fact: "I would rather have questions that can't be answered than answers that can't be questioned." — American theoretical physicist who won the Nobel Prize for his work on quantum electrodynamics.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Niels Bohr
info_cards.fact: "An expert is a person who has made all the mistakes that can be made in a very narrow field." — Danish physicist who made foundational contributions to understanding atomic structure and quantum theory.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Max Planck
info_cards.fact: "Science cannot solve the ultimate mystery of nature." — German physicist whose work founded quantum theory, for which he won the Nobel Prize.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Werner Heisenberg
info_cards.fact: "What we observe is not nature itself, but nature exposed to our method of questioning." — German physicist known for the uncertainty principle, a cornerstone of quantum mechanics.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Dmitri Mendeleev
info_cards.fact: "There is nothing in this world that I fear more than to have my words exceed my deeds." — Russian chemist who created the periodic table of elements, predicting the existence of undiscovered elements.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Michael Faraday
info_cards.fact: "Nothing is too wonderful to be true." — British scientist whose discoveries in electromagnetism led to the invention of the electric motor.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: James Clerk Maxwell
info_cards.fact: "The true logic of this world is in the calculus of probabilities." — Scottish physicist whose equations unified electricity, magnetism, and light into one theory of electromagnetism.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Gregor Mendel
info_cards.fact: "Nature... follows established laws... and the same laws must... be applicable to all variable organisms." — Austrian monk and scientist whose pea-plant experiments founded the science of genetics.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Louis Pasteur
info_cards.fact: "Chance favors the prepared mind." — French scientist who developed the process of pasteurization and helped establish the germ theory of disease.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Alexander Fleming
info_cards.fact: "One sometimes finds what one is not looking for." — Scottish scientist who discovered penicillin, the first widely used antibiotic.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Edward Jenner
info_cards.fact: "I should be ill indeed if I did not feel myself fully repaid by the enjoyment of the present." — English physician who developed the first vaccine, protecting against smallpox.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Ada Lovelace
info_cards.fact: "That brain of mine is something more than merely mortal; as time will show." — English mathematician regarded as the first computer programmer for her work on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Alan Turing
info_cards.fact: "Sometimes it is the people no one imagines anything of who do the things that no one can imagine." — British mathematician whose work laid the foundations of computer science and helped break Nazi codes in WWII.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Grace Hopper
info_cards.fact: "It's easier to ask forgiveness than it is to get permission." — American computer scientist and Navy admiral who helped develop one of the earliest programming languages, COBOL.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Tim Berners-Lee
info_cards.fact: "This is for everyone." — British computer scientist who invented the World Wide Web in 1989.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Steve Jobs
info_cards.fact: "Your time is limited, so don't waste it living someone else's life." — American entrepreneur who co-founded Apple Inc. and helped popularize personal computers and smartphones.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Bill Gates
info_cards.fact: "It's fine to celebrate success but it is more important to heed the lessons of failure." — American entrepreneur who co-founded Microsoft and later focused on global health and education philanthropy.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Hedy Lamarr
info_cards.fact: "Hope and curiosity about the future seemed better than guarantees." — Austrian-American actress and inventor whose frequency-hopping work helped lay groundwork for modern wireless technology.

lessons.title: World Leaders and History Makers
lessons.subject: General Knowledge
learning_objectives: Identify influential historical and modern figures
lessons.reading_material: Throughout history, individuals have changed the world. Malala Yousafzai fought for girls' education. Nelson Mandela ended apartheid in South Africa. Marie Curie won two Nobel Prizes in science. Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) transformed the Arabian Peninsula with Islam. These figures inspire us through courage, perseverance, and service to others. Leadership means taking responsibility for others, not just having power.
practical_activities: Class timeline: each student researches one figure and places them on a world history timeline
exercises: Name three people who changed history and explain each person's contribution
What makes someone a 'history maker'?
Why is Malala important to girls around the world?
lessons.homework: Write a one-page biography of someone you consider a history maker — can be a local hero.

revision.notes: History makers change society through courage, ideas, or service. Legacy = lasting impact.
revision.tip: Think about local heroes too — impact does not have to be global.

lessons.assessment: Compare the contributions of two history makers from different continents.

lessons.title: Nutrition and Balanced Meals
lessons.subject: Cooking
lessons.reading_material: The five main food groups are: Carbohydrates (bread, rice, pasta — energy), Proteins (meat, fish, eggs, beans — growth and repair), Dairy (milk, cheese — calcium for bones), Fruits and Vegetables (vitamins and minerals), Fats and Sugars (energy in small amounts). A balanced meal includes foods from each group. The Eatwell Plate (UK) or MyPlate (USA) visually shows healthy proportions. Fibre (from vegetables and whole grains) aids digestion.
practical_activities: Design a healthy weekly meal plan covering all 5 food groups
exercises: Name the 5 food groups and one food from each
Which nutrient builds and repairs muscles?
Why is fibre important?
lessons.homework: Analyse your last three meals — which food groups were present and which were missing?

revision.notes: 5 groups: Carbs, Proteins, Dairy, Fruits/Veg, Fats/Sugars. Balance = something from each group.
revision.tip: Half your plate should be fruit and vegetables.

quiz.question: Which food group provides the most energy?

lessons.assessment: Plan a healthy lunch and dinner — identify which food groups each meal covers.

lessons.title: Food and Daily Routines in Arabic

lessons.title: Trade and Interdependence
lessons.unit: How Countries Depend on Each Other
lessons.subject: Social Studies
lessons.reading_material: No country can produce everything its people need. Countries specialise in what they produce best and trade with others. Imports are goods brought into a country; exports are goods sent out. For example, Saudi Arabia exports oil; Bangladesh exports textiles; Japan exports technology. This interdependence means countries rely on each other. Trade creates jobs and lowers prices, but it can also create dependency and inequality if some countries get unfair deals.
practical_activities: Map activity: trace where 10 everyday objects come from — stick labels on a world map
exercises: Define import and export with examples from your country
Why do countries specialise?
Give one advantage and one disadvantage of global trade
lessons.homework: Check the labels on five items at home — where were they made? Create a table.

revision.notes: Import = bought from abroad. Export = sold abroad. Interdependence = countries need each other.
revision.tip: Check product labels — nearly everything involves global trade.

lessons.title: Supply and Demand
lessons.subject: Business Studies
learning_objectives: Describe how price is set in a market
lessons.reading_material: Supply is the amount of a product that sellers are willing to sell. Demand is the amount buyers want to buy. When demand goes up and supply stays the same, prices tend to rise. When supply is high and demand is low, prices fall. This balance is called market equilibrium. Understanding supply and demand helps us predict prices in everyday markets.
practical_activities: Role-play a market: half the class are 'sellers', half 'buyers' — negotiate a price for stickers
exercises: If apples become scarce, what happens to price?

lessons.homework: Visit a local market and observe what items seem plentiful or scarce. Write a short paragraph.

revision.notes: Supply = how much sellers offer; Demand = how much buyers want. Prices rise when demand exceeds supply.
revision.tip: Relate to something you buy regularly — does price change by season?
